# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is lazy. Left alone, it sits still, and when it does move, it only flows downhill. Everything about a municipal water system is an elaborate argument against this laziness—a chain of engineered nudges that convinces water to climb thirty stories into a showerhead at 6 a.m. To understand how this works, let's follow water through a concrete example: a fictional but realistic city we'll call Meridian, home to a reservoir, a treatment plant, and the Harrow Tower, a 32-story apartment building downtown.

## The Fundamental Currency: Elevation as Pressure

The single most important concept in water distribution is *head*—the energy water carries by virtue of its elevation. Every 2.31 feet of height corresponds to one pound per square inch (psi) of pressure. This is why cities historically built water towers on hills and why engineers speak of "hydraulic grade lines" the way accountants speak of balance sheets: water will only flow to points below that line unless you add energy somewhere.
